label: Riemannian Metrics
notes: This chapter, printed pages nine through fifty-four, installs the single piece of structure that turns a bare smooth manifold into a place where we measure. A Riemannian metric is a smoothly varying inner product, and from it lengths, angles, and distance all follow naturally. Open the lecture by stressing this promotion from smooth to geometric.

label: Definition of a Metric
notes: A Riemannian metric is a smooth symmetric two-tensor field that is positive definite at every point. Symmetry and positive definiteness make each fiber a genuine inner product, while smoothness ties neighboring inner products together so that everything we build varies differentiably across the manifold. Emphasize all three conditions explicitly.

label: Components in Coordinates
notes: In any chart the metric is recorded by the symmetric matrix of components g sub i j, the inner products of coordinate vector fields. Positive definiteness of this matrix at each point is exactly the local condition we verify, and the matrix changes by the usual tensor transformation law between overlapping charts.

label: Inner-Product Ellipses
notes: Visualize the metric as a field of unit balls, one ellipse per point describing which tangent vectors have length one. Where the ellipse is small the metric is large and the manifold feels stretched; the smooth deformation of these ellipses across the region is precisely the geometry that the metric encodes.

label: Norm and Length of Curves
notes: The metric gives each tangent vector a norm, and integrating the speed of a curve against that norm produces its length. This length is independent of how the curve is parametrized, so it is a genuine geometric quantity attached to the image of the path rather than to the clock used to traverse it.

label: Musical Isomorphisms
notes: Positive definiteness lets the metric convert vectors into covectors and back. Lowering an index with flat sends a vector field to a one-form; raising with sharp inverts the operation. These musical isomorphisms identify the tangent and cotangent bundles canonically and let us define the gradient as the sharp of the differential.

label: Pullback Metrics
notes: A smooth map with injective differential pulls a metric back to its domain by feeding pushed-forward vectors into the target inner product. When the map is an immersion the pullback stays positive definite, which is exactly how submanifolds inherit their induced Riemannian metric, the first fundamental form, from an ambient space.

label: Isometries
notes: An isometry is a diffeomorphism whose pullback returns the original metric, so it preserves all lengths and angles. Local isometries relax this requirement to neighborhoods of each point. The isometries of a manifold form a group, and deciding when two Riemannian manifolds are isometric is a central problem the rest of the book attacks.

label: Existence by Partitions of Unity
notes: Every smooth manifold admits a Riemannian metric. Choose Euclidean metrics in coordinate patches, then glue them with a partition of unity subordinate to the cover. Because a convex combination of positive-definite forms remains positive definite, the patched object is a smooth global metric defined everywhere on the manifold.

label: Riemannian Distance
notes: Define the distance between two points as the infimum of lengths of admissible curves joining them. This distance is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and vanishes only on the diagonal, making a connected Riemannian manifold into a genuine metric space. Note that an infimum need not be achieved by any single curve.

label: The Metric Topology
notes: A key theorem says the topology induced by the Riemannian distance agrees with the original manifold topology. So no new open sets appear and none are lost: the analytic distance and the smooth structure see the same neighborhoods, which keeps later limit and continuity arguments honest and well grounded throughout the theory.

label: Product and Warped Metrics
notes: New metrics arise from old ones. A product manifold carries the direct sum of its factor metrics, while a warped product scales one factor by a positive function defined on the other. Warped products model surfaces of revolution and cosmological spacetimes with a single flexible construction worth keeping in mind for examples.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We turned a smooth manifold into a measured space: a positive-definite tensor gives norms, lengths, musical isomorphisms, distance, and a matching topology, all transported by isometries. With metrics in hand the next chapters can finally differentiate vector fields through connections and define curvature, the true subject of the course.
